prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock alone, with Katori and Ye, and the first round has made me more confident, not less. Six of eight members now prefer this configuration, but I do not rely on that count. What matters is that the reasons given are independent. Danielsson, Kroll, Johansson, Mehlig and Pearce each reach it from a different starting point, and none of them found a missing principal among the two names. The physics is a single bounded idea with a measured result. Katori's magic-wavelength condition removes the differential light shift that would otherwise destroy a trapped-atom clock, and it lets very many atoms be probed at once, free of Doppler and recoil shifts. Ye's group showed what that buys: instability and systematic uncertainty near 10^-18, operation with a degenerate spin-polarised Fermi gas, and centimetre-scale gravitational time dilation measured within one sample. The result is cross-checked by independent clocks, so maturity is not in question. As an atomic theorist I can say that the 10^-18 budget is credible because the polarisabilities, blackbody-radiation shift and higher-order light shifts are well controlled. I would phrase the citation around the lattice clock itself, not optical clocks in general and not the applications, so that it commits us neither to ion clocks nor to the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against is still overlap and credit. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and precision spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions, so a reader can say precision optical metrology has been honoured twice already. I answer that neither citation contains the magic-wavelength lattice, but Olsson is right that I cannot make the overlap vanish; I can only keep the wording narrow. Second, Ye's contribution is partly the pushing of accuracy, and I accept that a purist could call that refinement. I weigh it as the demonstration that the concept works at the limit, which is how experiments usually decide a concept. Third, ion-clock pioneers, the early Sr and Yb groups and the ultrastable-laser developers fall outside two names, and that is a real attribution cost. Fourth, the redefinition of the second is still pending and many fundamental-physics payoffs are prospective, as Pearce says. I judge these costs smaller than the unresolved credit problems on B057, B041, B036 and B054, but they are not zero.

responses.point: Olsson ranks spherical-aberration correction (B053) first but says she would not insist on it, and argues that Ye's contribution to the clock is partly the pushing of accuracy and that the 2005 prize already covers much enabling frequency metrology.
responses.response: I think you are right that the committee must not treat the safe choice as proof of the best one, and I appreciate that you apply the same test to your own candidate. On substance, I do not think the overlap with 2005 is as large as it looks. Hall and Haensch gave us a way to count optical cycles. What makes a lattice clock work is a different thing: holding a large ensemble in a state where the clock transition is not perturbed by the trap. Ye's group did more than push accuracy. They resolved the systematics that this concept made visible, such as the blackbody shift, and used the many-atom sample for new measurements. That is a share of the discovery itself, not just engineering polish. I do accept your point that the citation must be tight. On B053, I see the corrector as a real invention with traceable authorship, but Krivanek's omission and the instrument-versus-discovery question make it harder for me than the clock.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B057 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as his preferred part, framing the citation around the Z2 classification and the observation of the quantum spin Hall state, and rejected my description of it as overdue because that concerns timing and not credit.
responses.response: I accept your correction. 'Overdue' was an argument about timing, and it was the wrong kind of argument. I withdraw it. The question for B057 is whether a narrowly worded citation on the Z2 insulator and its HgTe realisation withstands the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D contributors. You argue that it does, and the Kane-Mele and Molenkamp parts are indeed original and confirmed. I still land differently, for two reasons. The HgTe proposal is what made the experiment possible, so I do not think the allocation can be separated from the observation. And a three-person limit forces us to leave out people who plausibly stand on both sides of that line. For the clock the equivalent question has a short answer. If the committee finds the clock blocked, B057 is where I would go, and your framing is how I would word it.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from IceCube to the clock, weights the instrument case over the scientific-reach argument, and holds B041 as his first alternative, saying he would revisit it if a defensible credit exists.
responses.response: I agree that I should not lean too hard on time-dilation tests and dark-matter searches, which are mostly prospective. My case rests on the instrument and its demonstrated performance, so I am content to be held to that. On B041 I asked in round 1 for an astroparticle view on whether Halzen and Karle are the decisive pair, and your own round-1 text says that a two-person credit for a large collaboration with AMANDA ancestry is only defensible. If you or Danielsson can show that the pair is decisive, I would revisit, and I have kept the discovery argument in mind. At present neither of you has said that, so I keep B041 behind the clock on attribution. I would not call this a verdict on the science; the diffuse flux is secure.

responses.point: Danielsson holds the clock first, says that narrow framing protects against the comb overlap without removing it, and wants the committee to say explicitly that the clock is a new concept built on the comb and ultrastable-laser toolkit.
responses.response: Your point is fair and I want it recorded: Ye's clocks depend on comb technology and on ultrastable lasers that others developed, and the clock is a new concept built on that toolkit, not an independent one. I think that is acceptable because every instrument stands on earlier tools, and the 1997/2001, 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured parts of that toolkit and not the magic-wavelength lattice. I would still resist your suggestion in round 1 that my familiarity with the field is a reason to weigh my systematics judgement heavily, if it means the others defer. The argument should stand without that. For the final text I propose the citation 'for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock', with the 10^-18 result as supporting wording.

responses.point: Mehlig supports the clock, asks whether the pending redefinition of the second argues for waiting or for acting now, and wants the citation put in terms of the invention and not the applications.
responses.response: On your question: I think it is irrelevant to the physics and should neither delay nor drive the decision. The redefinition is a metrological decision taken by others, on the strength of results that are already independently established. If we waited for it we would be treating a bureaucratic step as a scientific condition, and if we acted because of it we would be anticipating a decision that is not ours. That is also why I accept your wording point and have kept applications out of the proposed citation. Your remark that the many-body Fermi-gas operation is itself a statistical-physics result is something I would keep in the discussion text, since it answers the claim that this is only metrology.

uncertainties: How far the committee thinks the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-ion prize already cover precision optical metrology; I judge them distinct but cannot show that to everyone's satisfaction.
Whether the early Sr and Yb lattice groups, ion-clock pioneers or ultrastable-laser developers have a claim that two names cannot represent.
Whether a two-part configuration with B057 or B032 is possible inside three names; with the supplied credits it is not, so I propose B027 alone.
My recollection of clock performance numbers and priority dates is not checked against sources at this stage.
statement.conflict_note: From my profile, my attosecond work involves collaborations with the Lund group and ETH Zurich (Keller), and I am an atomic theorist, so I remain in the same broad field as B027. My profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye, nor with any credited name in B057 or B032, so I see no specific recusal issue. I note that I have a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, who is not on any shortlisted credit, and I would recuse from any candidate that involved the people named in my profile. I have no new conflict to disclose in round 2. I think my field proximity should be weighed by the committee, not treated as grounds for recusal on B027.
